summaries.text: You are currently teaching in the computer science engineering department at IIT Kharagpur. This course on computer networks will consist of 40 lectures.
We will be covering the emergence of computer networks and their brief history. The lecture will also introduce the protocols and reference models that provide an abstract view of computer networks.

A computer network consists of multiple nodes connected by communication lines, allowing indirect communication between nodes that are not directly connected. Network devices, such as switches and routers, are also included in this definition and are not necessarily computers themselves.

Network devices such as switches and routers facilitate communication and are considered nodes in the network. Computers can communicate with each other, exchanging various types of information, including data, programs, or other kinds of information.

Computers can be connected to perform large computations by breaking down the work into smaller pieces and assigning them to individual computers. This can be a cost-effective alternative to using a single, powerful computer.

Computers can now be used for communication, including sending emails, voice calls, and video calls, which are becoming increasingly popular and fast ways to stay in touch. The computer network is now also referred to as a platform for communication, with many applications converging onto it.

Computer networks are being used to support distributed systems, such as a railway reservation system, where functionality is distributed across different locations to avoid queues. This is another application of networks, with examples including distributed databases and other types of applications.

The first commercial computer, an Univac, was installed in 1948 and by 1958, the first US communication satellite became operational. In 1964, a packet switching network was proposed for an airline reservation system by the RAND Corporation, and in 1969, ARPANET, the first packet switching network, was developed.

The RAND Corporation proposed a packet switching network in the 1960s, which led to the development of ARPANET. The first computer chip was introduced in 1971, a 4-bit chip with 2300 transistors, and Ethernet specifications were formulated in 1972.
In 1974, IBM introduced its own network, SNA, and in 1975, the Altair 8800, the first commercial microcomputer, was sold as a kit.
The first commercial spreadsheet, the VC calc, was introduced in 1979. IBM PC/XT, with one floppy drive, was introduced in 1981, later upgraded to include a second floppy and a hard drive.
IBM releases a multitasking OS for PCs in an unspecified year. Microsoft releases Windows, a multitasking system, and the NSF takes over as the internet's backbone, replacing ARPANET, in 1989.

Commercial companies began to take an interest in the network as more people joined, leading to the development of more user-friendly and feature-rich tools. The World Wide Web, invented in 1991, became the "killer app" that drew a large number of users to the network.
Microsoft had its own web browser, Microsoft Explorer, which added to the growing number of options. The "dot com meltdown" in 2000 brought the frenzy of growth to a halt.

We wanted distributed systems to be able to communicate with each other, so this project was born. The subnet of Honeywell IMPs, connected by 64 kbps lines, allowed various computers and terminals to communicate with each other.

The NSF upgraded their system with a new backbone connecting supercomputing centres to regional networks, increasing speeds from 64 kbps to 1.5 mbps. This upgraded backbone allowed fast communication with hundreds of thousands of universities, research labs, and libraries.

Startup companies, often founded by young engineers with innovative ideas, have played a major role in driving the growth of computing networks. Their success has sparked widespread interest and innovation in the field, fueling an explosive growth in computer networks throughout the 90s and into the 21st century.

The growth in computer networks has continued despite the dot com bubble bursting in 2000. The concept of a computer network can be thought of as a number of nodes, including computers and devices, connected by communication lines.
Computer networks can have a direct point-to-point connection between nodes, with communication going in one or both directions.

Nodes can communicate with each other simultaneously, allowing data to be exchanged in both directions at the same time. In some cases, a single point-to-point medium can be shared among multiple nodes, enabling communication among multiple nodes connected to a single line.

Multiplexing allows multiple people to share a single point-to-point link, enabling multiple nodes to communicate at the same time. Additionally, there are other types of links, such as broadcast links, which can be used for one-to-many communication, like satellite communication or broadcasting TV signals.

A broadcast medium can be dedicated to one user or shared among multiple users, in which case it's known as a multiple access medium. When nodes are physically distributed over the broadcast medium, protocols are needed to share the medium, and this is also called multiple access.

The lecturer is explaining that multicasting is a type of communication that sends information to a specified group, sitting between broadcasting and point-to-point communication. The lecturer is also discussing how computer networks are typically divided into local, metropolitan, and wide area networks, with local area networks being limited to a small area such as one building.

Local area networks are typically privately owned, allowing for uniform policies to be applied across the network. In contrast, wide area networks often involve multiple, independently owned nodes with differing policies.

Metropolitan area networks serve a community or city and present issues with access, particularly how to connect geographically dispersed locations. Connecting these locations can be costly, similar to wide area networks, but is still less expensive than long-distance communication.
The cost of long-distance communication has decreased over time due to improved technology and increased volume of users, allowing more people to access networks.

Wide area network costs are still a significant issue, but they enable connection between multiple local area networks, forming a network of networks or the internet. Protocols are needed in networks because different people have different ideas about how things should be done, and protocols standardise these processes.

Protocols are a common basis for communication between people with different ideas about how things should be done, standardising processes so they can interact. Each protocol has two interfaces: a service interface defining operations and a peer-to-peer interface defining messages exchanged with other peers.

The peer interface defines the messages exchanged between peers, enabling them to communicate with each other through the protocol. The protocol requires resources from other layers, indicating a layered architecture.

The layers of a computer network are broken up into different functionalities, with each layer having a specific job to achieve smooth functioning. The layers are stacked on top of each other, with each layer interacting with its peers through a protocol and its adjacent layers through a service interface.

Each layer maintains a virtual connection with the corresponding layer in a peer for running peer-to-peer protocols. The task of each layer can be broken down into sub-tasks, with some sub-tasks potentially delegated to lower layers.

The peer-to-peer protocol runs between corresponding layers in the same node using a well-defined interface and a virtual connection. A virtual connection is an indirect connection, not necessarily a physical one, that allows communication between layers in different nodes.

The peer-to-peer protocol uses an indirect connection that hops from node to node, allowing communication between layers in different nodes. Despite appearing as direct communication, the actual exchange is virtual, with physical communication only occurring at the lowest layer.

The physical connection between nodes can be made through various mediums, such as wire, fiber optic links, or satellite links. The implementation of each layer in each node is transparent to other nodes, allowing for flexibility in how each layer is executed.

Companies X and Y can implement the same services in different ways as long as they agree on the protocol and interface between layers. Nodes can also have peer relationships, allowing different machines, such as IBM and Sun computers, to communicate with each other.

Nodes from different companies, such as Sun and IBM, can have a peer-to-peer relationship even if they have different operating systems and processors, as long as they agree on the protocol. This allows for innovation and development as long as the protocol and interface standards are followed.

The focus is on abstracting out the unnecessary complexity of specific implementations to concentrate on the protocols, interfaces, and functionalities. The goal is to gain a general understanding of networking before delving into the details of specific module development.

Protocols between peer layers can be changed if all peers agree, but doing so won't affect other layers. The service definition specifies what a layer does without detailing its implementation, and the interface defines how to access the layer's functions.

The lecturer is discussing different layered models, mentioning the OSI reference model and TCP/IP reference model as the most widely used. The OSI model is considered somewhat theoretical, whereas the TCP/IP model is widely adopted and used in various networking technologies.

The lecturer is explaining that the layered models are also referred to as protocol stacks and exist in various forms, with TCP/IP becoming more widely accepted than the OSI model. The OSI model is being described with its seven layers, including the physical layer, network layer, and application layer.

The lecturer is explaining that the seven layers of the OSI model each have specific functionalities that work together to provide the network's overall functionality. The lecturer is also describing the process of peer-to-peer communication, where a message travels down the layers on the sending machine, each layer adding a header before reaching the physical layer.

The application layer initiates communication and is responsible for providing protocols such as telnet, which allows a client to connect to a server on another machine. A telnet client and server are both located in the application layer and facilitate communication between machines.

The telnet client and server know only about the protocol at the application layer, without needing to know about lower-layer details. The application layer hands over the data to be sent to the lower layer in the same node, which then runs its own protocol with the target machine.

As the data moves down the stack, each layer adds its own protocol's message to the original data, making it larger at each step. This process continues until the physical layer, where the data is sent to the remote machine, then it moves back up the stack, with each layer removing its message as it goes.

The protocol messages are passed up through each layer on the receiving side, with each layer reading the corresponding header it received from its peer on the source machine. Two machines with different operating systems, such as a DOS machine and a Macintosh, can still communicate with each other.

The presentation layer adds its own header to the original data, making it "fatter", which is then passed to the session layer. The headers added by each layer are stripped off as the data travels down the layers on the receiving machine.

The seven protocol layers are being discussed from bottom up, with the physical link being the first, responsible for transmitting bits. The data link layer follows, focusing on transmitting frames and enabling direct communication between two connected nodes.

The network layer ensures packets are routed correctly through the network by keeping track of the route. The transport layer is responsible for sending packets to the application, and packets are created by breaking down the data into manageable segments.

The transport layer creates packets from data received from the upper layer. The session, presentation, and application layers manage the connection and encode/decode messages, while the application layer contains various protocols, such as FTP, Telnet, and HTTP, that enable specific tasks.

The FTP, HTTP, and SMTP protocols enable specific tasks such as file transfer, web browsing, and email sending. The application layer requires a reliable and cheap connection to its peer, ensuring stable communication between systems.

The presentation layer handles protocol conversion, data translation, compression, and encryption, preparing the data for transmission. The session layer establishes a connection between applications and computers, allowing for a continuous flow of data and enabling features like checkpoints and dialogue control.

The transport layer accepts data from the layer above, splits it into smaller packets if necessary, and ensures these packets arrive correctly and in the right order at the other end. The transport layer can provide different types of transport services, including error-free point-to-point channels or cheaper alternatives, such as broadcasting to multiple destinations.

The data link layer controls broadcasting and handles technological mismatches, error correction, and billing information, making the physical layer appear like a pure transmission channel. The data link layer is the lowest layer above the physical layer, which transmits raw bits.

The OSI reference model and TCP/IP are the most common protocols used, with the OSI model providing an abstract view of networking. The network topology will be discussed, with the lecturer explaining what is meant by a network topology in the next part of the lecture.

A computer network consists of nodes connected by communication links, forming a graph with a certain structure. This structure implies how communication will take place, but it's generally not feasible for direct one-to-one communication between each pair of nodes.

The lecturer is discussing LAN topologies, specifically mentioning the bus topology as the first to cover, describing it as simple. The bus topology is a type of LAN topology that allows communication between nodes by transmitting signals over a single shared cable.

The bus topology allows point-to-point communication between nodes, but this requires each pair of communicating nodes to temporarily use the shared link. Other nodes ignore the communication, but all nodes receive the transmission anyway, making it non-private.
Nodes ignore communications not addressed to them but may copy relevant information. A distributed protocol is needed to decide which nodes can use the shared link to communicate with each other.
